content: Bipolar disorder is a psychiatric condition characterized by alternating episodes of elevated or irritable mood (manic or hypomanic episodes) and episodes of depressed mood with diminished energy (depressive episodes). The primary approach to managing acute mania involves pharmacological treatment, with the initial goal being the rapid control of agitation, aggression, and potentially dangerous behaviors. Aripiprazole, classified as an atypical antipsychotic, is utilized in the treatment of mania either as a standalone therapy or in combination with other medications. According to the British Association of Psychopharmacology guidelines, placebo-controlled trials of atypical antipsychotics, including aripiprazole, have demonstrated their efficacy in managing acute manic or mixed episodes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of aripiprazole, either as monotherapy or in combination with other antimanic agents, in comparison to placebo or other pharmacological treatments for alleviating acute symptoms of manic or mixed episodes. Additional aims included assessing the acceptability of aripiprazole treatment, identifying its adverse effects, and determining mortality rates among individuals receiving this medication. The review included a comprehensive search of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) up to July 31, 2013, using databases such as The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO, as well as clinical trial registries like those of Bristol-Myers Squibb, the World Health Organization (WHO), and ClinicalTrials.gov. The selection criteria focused on RCTs comparing aripiprazole with placebo or other drugs for the treatment of acute manic or mixed episodes. Data extraction and bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers, and missing data were sought from trial authors or the drug manufacturer. A total of 10 studies involving 3,340 participants were included in the review. Seven studies compared aripiprazole monotherapy with placebo (2,239 participants), with two of these studies including a third comparison group—one with lithium (485 participants) and the other with haloperidol (480 participants). Two studies evaluated aripiprazole as an adjunctive treatment to valproate or lithium versus placebo as an adjunctive treatment (754 participants), and one study compared aripiprazole with haloperidol (347 participants). The overall risk of bias in the included studies was unclear. A high dropout rate (greater than 20% for each intervention in eight trials) may have influenced the reliability of the efficacy estimates. Evidence indicated that aripiprazole was more effective than placebo in reducing manic symptoms in both adults and children/adolescents at three and four weeks, but not at six weeks. This was measured using the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS), with a mean difference (MD) at three weeks of -3.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] -5.82 to -2.05; six studies; N = 1,819; moderate-quality evidence), representing a modest improvement. When compared to other drug treatments, such as lithium or haloperidol, no statistically significant differences in the reduction of manic symptoms were observed at three weeks (YMRS MD 0.07, 95% CI -1.24 to 1.37; three studies; N = 972; moderate-quality evidence) or at any other time point up to 12 weeks. Aripiprazole was associated with a higher incidence of movement disorders compared to placebo, as measured by the Simpson Angus Scale (SAS), the Barnes Akathisia Scale (BAS), and participant-reported akathisia. This finding was supported by high-quality evidence, with more individuals requiring anticholinergic medication (risk ratio [RR] 3.28, 95% CI 1.82 to 5.91; two studies; N = 730; high-quality evidence). Additionally, aripiprazole caused more gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea (high-quality evidence) and constipation, and led to a higher proportion of children and adolescents experiencing prolactin levels below the normal range. Significant heterogeneity was observed in the meta-analysis of movement disorders associated with aripiprazole and other treatments, likely due to the differing side effect profiles of lithium and haloperidol. At the three-week time point, meta-analysis was not feasible due to insufficient data. However, by 12 weeks, haloperidol was associated with significantly more movement disorders than aripiprazole, as measured by the SAS, BAS, and Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS), as well as participant-reported akathisia. By 12 weeks, no differences were observed between aripiprazole and lithium in terms of movement disorders (SAS, BAS, AIMS), except for participant-reported akathisia, which was more common with aripiprazole (RR 2.97, 95% CI 1.37 to 6.43; one study; N = 313). In conclusion, aripiprazole is an effective treatment for mania in adults, children, and adolescents. However, its use is associated with gastrointestinal disturbances and movement disorders. The limited number of comparative trials with medications other than haloperidol and lithium makes it difficult to determine the precise role of aripiprazole in the therapeutic management of acute mania.
